history.heading: Whalers and explorers
paragraphs: South Georgia and the South Sandwich Islands lie in the remote South Atlantic. James Cook landed on South Georgia in 1775 and claimed it for Britain. Sealers hunted fur and elephant seals in the 19th century.

From 1904 South Georgia became a centre of Antarctic whaling, with stations such as Grytviken, where hundreds of thousands of whales were processed until the 1960s. In 1916 Ernest Shackleton crossed the island's mountains to reach help after his ship Endurance was crushed in the ice; he died there in 1922 and is buried at Grytviken. Argentine forces landed in 1982, and their recapture by Britain was part of the Falklands War.

culture.heading: No permanent population
paragraphs: There is no permanent population. Scientists of the British Antarctic Survey and government officers live at King Edward Point and Bird Island, and a small museum operates at Grytviken. The islands host enormous colonies of king penguins, fur seals, elephant seals and albatrosses.

politics.heading: British Overseas Territory
paragraphs: The islands are a British Overseas Territory administered by a commissioner who is also the Governor of the Falkland Islands. Argentina claims them as part of its territory.

economy.heading: Fishing and conservation
paragraphs: Revenue comes from fishing licences for toothfish and krill, tourism from cruise ships and the sale of stamps. A major rat eradication project, completed in 2018, helped restore seabird populations. The surrounding waters form a large marine protected area.
